subject: Agriculture
title: The Irish Potato Famine
description: A quick, practical guide to The Irish Potato Famine.

hook.text: In 1845, a water mold destroyed Ireland's potato crop. One million died and another million emigrated.

buildup.text: Ireland's poor depended almost entirely on one potato variety—the Irish Lumper. It was a genetic monoculture.

discovery.text: Phytophthora infestans—potato late blight—arrived from North America and spread across Europe in weeks.

twist.text: British policies worsened the disaster. Ireland exported food during the famine—grain left while people starved.

climax.text: The famine reshaped Ireland permanently—halving its population and fueling Irish immigration worldwide.

punchline.text: One crop, one disease, one nation transformed forever.

quiz.question: What organism caused the Irish Potato Famine?
options: Phytophthora infestans, a water mold causing late blight

details.summary: The Irish Potato Famine of 1845-1852 was caused by Phytophthora infestans, a water mold that destroyed potato crops across Ireland. The resulting famine killed over one million people and forced another million to emigrate, reshaping Irish society and global understanding of crop disease risk.
details.whyItMatters: The Irish Famine demonstrated how reliance on a single crop variety makes entire populations vulnerable to disease. It remains the most cited example of the catastrophic intersection of plant pathology, monoculture, and political failure.
takeaways: Phytophthora infestans destroyed up to 75% of Ireland's potato crop repeatedly
Over one million people died and another million emigrated during 1845-1852
The disaster resulted from extreme dependence on a single genetically uniform crop

faq.question: What caused the Irish Potato Famine?
faq.answer: The water mold Phytophthora infestans arrived in Ireland from the Americas and destroyed potato crops. Ireland's rural poor depended almost entirely on one potato variety, the Irish Lumper, which had no resistance. Cool, wet Irish weather was ideal for the pathogen's spread.

faq.question: What lessons did the Irish Famine teach about crop disease?
faq.answer: The Famine showed that genetic uniformity in crops creates catastrophic vulnerability to disease. It demonstrated the importance of crop diversity, food system resilience, and the danger of political indifference. It also launched the scientific field of plant pathology.
